title: Reference Call Brief Template (Internal)
body:
Purpose
Use this 1–2 page internal brief to prep a customer reference call. The goal is to (1) make the reference customer feel set up and respected, (2) keep the call on-message and compliant, and (3) capture outcomes back to HubSpot for reporting.

How to use
- Copy this doc for each call: “Reference Call Brief — [Customer] x [Prospect] — [YYYY-MM-DD]”.
- Share internally with AE/CSM/SE at least 24 hours before the call.
- Do NOT forward to the customer or prospect as-is (contains internal notes). If the customer requests an agenda, send a simplified agenda only.

SECTION 1: Call basics
- Reference customer: [Company name]
- Deployment type(s) with Redwood: [Hosted API / Dedicated / Private (VPC/on-prem)]
- Primary use case(s): [e.g., RAG summarization, chat assistant, search/rerank, embeddings]
- Prospect company: [Company name]
- Prospect segment: [Startup / Mid-market / Enterprise]
- Deal stage: [Discovery / Eval / Security review / Procurement / Negotiation]
- Date/time (incl time zones): [ ]
- Duration: [30 min / 45 min]
- Meeting link / dial-in: [ ]

Attendees
- Reference customer attendees (names/titles):
  - [ ]
- Prospect attendees (names/titles):
  - [ ]
- Redwood attendees (names/roles):
  - AE: [ ]
  - CSM (required): [ ]
  - Solutions Eng (optional / recommended for technical buyers): [ ]

Objective (what “good” looks like)
- Primary objective (pick 1):
  - [ ] De-risk Dedicated/Private deployment (security, networking, reliability)
  - [ ] Validate performance economics (latency / throughput / unit cost)
  - [ ] Validate production readiness (observability, rollouts, fallbacks)
  - [ ] Confirm implementation effort and timeline
- Desired next step after call: [e.g., schedule technical deep dive, move to security review, confirm POC success criteria]

SECTION 2: Customer context (for Redwood attendees)
Customer overview (2–3 sentences)
- [What they do + why they’re a credible peer reference]

What they run on Redwood today
- Workload: [steady/bursty, interactive vs batch, typical context length]
- Models (public-safe names only): [e.g., “open-weight instruct model (70B class)” or “embedding model”]
- Regions / data residency constraints: [ ]
- Key platform features used:
  - [ ] Streaming
  - [ ] Function/tool calling / structured output
  - [ ] Batching
  - [ ] Prefix/KV caching
  - [ ] Routing / fallback policies
  - [ ] Console (dashboards, tracing, error analysis)
  - [ ] Optimize (recommendations / regression alerts)

Implementation snapshot
- Integration timeline: [e.g., “prototype in 2 days, prod in 3 weeks”]
- Architecture notes (internal): [Dedicated sizing, autoscaling policy, private networking, auth]
- Known sharp edges (be honest internally): [e.g., “initial prompt regression”, “needed guidance on caching config”]

Support / account health check (required)
- Account health: [Green / Yellow / Red]
- Open support issues that may come up: [list Jira/SUP links if applicable]
- Anything we should avoid due to recent escalations: [ ]

SECTION 3: Guardrails and permissions
Public vs private boundaries
- Approved to share (check what’s true for this customer):
  - [ ] Logo is approved publicly
  - [ ] Customer name can be used verbally on calls
  - [ ] Specific metrics can be shared as exact numbers
  - [ ] Metrics can be shared only as ranges (e.g., “~20–30% reduction”)
  - [ ] No metrics; qualitative only

Hard “do not share” list (confirm with CSM)
- [ ] Pricing, discounts, contract terms
- [ ] Non-public roadmap / upcoming features
- [ ] Security/compliance specifics beyond what’s already in signed/approved materials
- [ ] Proprietary customer data volumes or internal architecture details (unless explicitly approved)
- [ ] Competitive take-downs (keep it factual and respectful)

Reference load limits
- Max calls per month (if known): [e.g., 2]
- Cooldown after this call: [e.g., 2 weeks]
- Customer scheduling constraints: [e.g., “no Fridays”, “needs 7-day lead time”]

SECTION 4: What to emphasize (tailor to the prospect)
Choose 2–3 story pillars to anchor the call. Keep it concrete.

1) Performance economics (cost + latency)
- Suggested framing: “We needed predictable p95 latency while bringing unit cost down; Redwood gave us clear levers and visibility.”
- Proof points (customer-approved):
  - p95 latency before/after: [ ]
  - Throughput improvement (req/s or tokens/s): [ ]
  - Unit cost ($/1M tokens) or relative change: [ ]
  - What changed: [batching, caching, model choice, quantization profile]

2) Reliability + graceful degradation
- Suggested framing: “We could keep the app online during spikes/maintenance using routing + fallbacks.”
- Proof points:
  - Uptime target / SLA needs: [ ]
  - Fallback approach used: [model variant / region / capacity tier]
  - Operational practices: [alerts, runbooks, rollback policies]

3) Deployment flexibility (Hosted → Dedicated → Private)
- Suggested framing: “We started fast and then moved to a deployment mode that matched security + predictability needs.”
- Proof points:
  - Why Dedicated or Private: [data isolation, networking, compliance, predictable throughput]
  - Time/effort to migrate: [ ]
  - What stayed consistent: [same API surface, tooling, rollout controls]

4) Operational tooling (Console + Optimize)
- Suggested framing: “We could see exactly where time/cost went and catch regressions early.”
- Proof points:
  - Dashboards used: [latency by route/model, token breakdown]
  - Evals/regression monitoring: [prompt sets, alerts]

SECTION 5: “Avoid list” (common traps)
- Don’t over-claim (especially on security/compliance). Use approved language and qualify where needed.
- Don’t speculate on future features or timelines.
- Don’t compare vendors by name unless the customer initiates; even then keep it high-level.
- Don’t let the call become a Redwood product demo. The customer story is the asset.
- Don’t pressure the customer for additional commitments live (case study, webinar). Save for a separate follow-up.

SECTION 6: Suggested run-of-show (30 minutes)
0:00–0:03 Redwood intro + ground rules
- AE: quick intros, confirms timebox, reminds everyone it’s a peer conversation.
- CSM: states boundaries: “We’ll keep it high-level and avoid contract/pricing and anything confidential.”

0:03–0:08 Customer overview
- Customer: what they built, why they needed LLM inference, key constraints.

0:08–0:20 Deep dive on 2–3 pillars
- Guide the discussion to the prospect’s top risks.

0:20–0:27 Prospect Q&A
- Prospect asks; Redwood should avoid taking over unless clarification is needed.

0:27–0:30 Wrap
- AE thanks customer, confirms next step, ends on time.

SECTION 7: Q&A prompts
Questions to prep the reference customer (send separately as bullets if they want)
- What was the trigger that made inference a priority for you? (latency, cost, reliability, security)
- What did “success” look like for the first 30 days in production?
- What surprised you during implementation?
- What would you do differently if you started again?
- How do you measure latency/cost today (dashboards, KPIs, alerts)?
- How do you handle spikes, incidents, or model changes?

Likely prospect questions (pick those that match their stage)
Performance / scale
- What latency SLOs do you run, and how consistent is p95 under load?
- How did you approach batching/caching without hurting UX?
- What does throughput look like at peak?

Reliability
- Have you had outages or capacity constraints? How did fallbacks behave?
- What’s the operational overhead week-to-week?

Deployment / security (Dedicated/Private)
- Why did you choose Dedicated or Private vs hosted?
- How did security review go (VPC, KMS/HSM, audit logs)? What was easiest/hardest?
- How long did procurement + legal take?

Product / developer experience
- How long from first API call to production?
- What does observability look like for prompt failures/timeouts?

SECTION 8: Redwood internal prep checklist (complete before call)
- [ ] Confirm reference is approved for this call (CSM + AE ok).
- [ ] Confirm customer is not in a support escalation window.
- [ ] Confirm permissions: named customer ok? logo ok? metrics exact vs range?
- [ ] Provide customer a simple agenda + timebox (optional, recommended).
- [ ] Prepare 1-paragraph “why this prospect is a good peer” to motivate customer.
- [ ] Prep the opening script + boundaries.
- [ ] Have 2–3 approved proof points ready (or explicitly decide “qualitative only”).

SECTION 9: Post-call actions + logging (required)
Immediately after call (within same day)
1) Slack + internal recap
- Post a 5–8 bullet recap in: #sales (and #customer-success if relevant)
  - Who attended
  - Top 3 questions asked
  - Customer answers that landed well
  - Any risk surfaced (security, pricing, reliability)
  - Next step + owner

2) HubSpot logging (for reporting)
- Log an activity on the Prospect deal: “Reference Call — [Customer]”
- Include notes:
  - Call date/time
  - Reference customer used
  - Topics covered (latency/cost/reliability/security/deployment)
  - Outcome (helpful / neutral / negative) + why
  - Next step + date
- Update relevant fields (coordinate with RevOps if fields differ in your portal):
  - Reference call used? [Yes]
  - Reference customer name [ ]
  - Influence stage [Security / Procurement / Technical eval / Negotiation]
  - Reference call outcome [Positive / Mixed / Negative]

3) Thank-you + customer care
- AE/CSM sends a thank-you email to the reference customer.
- If incentives apply, notify program owner (Camila Reyes) and log against the reference program tracker.
- If customer expressed discomfort, CSM to follow up and apply cooldown.

Appendix: Copy/paste opening script (AE)
“Thanks everyone for joining. This is a peer-to-peer reference conversation. We’ll keep it high-level and avoid anything confidential, including pricing/contract terms and non-public roadmap. We’ll aim to end on time. [Customer], thanks again for helping—really appreciate it.”

Appendix: Copy/paste boundary reminder (CSM, as needed)
“Quick note: we can talk about outcomes and what worked, but we should avoid exact internal numbers unless we’ve explicitly agreed they’re shareable. Happy to describe ranges or qualitative impact.”
